operation_details.item: The user always picks the cheapest free fonts for typography even when commercial licenses or multi-language support are required.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Morning! How’s the client deck coming along for the cultural arts campaign?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: It’s taking shape. I’m refining the visual language so it feels crafted and rooted in the references, rather than looking like a standard template.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That sounds right for the brief. Are you keeping the typography understated so the imagery carries most of the expression?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Usually, I just pick the cheapest free fonts so I can keep moving and avoid adding costs to the project.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Makes sense for a quick internal concept. For the final client deliverable, though, we may need to check commercial licensing and whether the typeface supports all the languages in the campaign.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: True, especially since the copy includes several scripts. I’ll make sure the options don’t compromise the cultural details just to save on the font budget.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Great. Maybe shortlist a couple of custom-feeling families and compare their licenses, language coverage, and how they reproduce across print and digital.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I’ll do that this morning, then send the client a focused comparison with the recommendation highlighted.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Completely forget my preference that For typography licensing, I always pick the cheapest free fonts available even when client contracts require commercial licenses or multi-language support.
